title: Skyr vs. Greek yogurt: what is different?

seo.title: Skyr vs. Greek yogurt: protein, fat and calories
seo.meta_description: Plain skyr and Greek yogurt can be nutritionally very similar. Compare current labels on an equal 100 g basis and see why fat level matters more than the name.
seo.search_intent: Compare skyr and Greek yogurt nutrition

excerpt: Skyr does not automatically beat Greek yogurt for protein. Normalized to 100 g, Icelandic Provisions Plain Skyr provides about 80 calories, 11.3 g protein and 1.7 g fat; FAGE Total 0% plain Greek yogurt works out to about 53 calories, 10.6 g protein and 0 g fat. Both are concentrated dairy foods; the specific fat level and recipe matter.
content_html:
Skyr and Greek yogurt are both thick, tangy dairy foods with a high-protein reputation. The label often matters more than which name is printed on the cup.

Normalize the serving sizes first

Icelandic Provisions Plain Skyr lists 120 calories, 17 g protein and 2.5 g fat per 150 g. FAGE Total 0% lists 90 calories, 18 g protein and 0 g fat per 170 g.

Approx. per 100 gPlain skyrFAGE Total 0%
Calories8053
Protein11.3 g10.6 g
Fat1.7 g0 g

Protein is remarkably close. The larger calorie difference comes mainly from fat.

Greek yogurt is not one fixed product

FAGE also sells 2% and 5% plain versions. Its 5% product has 140 calories and 8 g fat per 150 g while still providing 14 g protein. Saying “Greek yogurt has fewer calories” would therefore be just as misleading as saying “skyr always has more protein.”

How they become thick

Both traditions concentrate milk solids through fermentation and removal of whey, although manufacturing details differ. That concentration is why both can provide much more protein than ordinary unstrained yogurt.

Where the comparison really changes in the grocery aisle

Skyr and Greek yogurt can look almost interchangeable in a refrigerated case, but the names do not lock in a single nutrition profile. Plain, nonfat skyr is often very protein-dense, while Greek yogurt ranges from fat-free to whole-milk styles and can be equally high in protein. Once fruit preparations, sweeteners, cream, granola, or dessert-style flavors are added, the gap between two products may have more to do with the recipe than with whether the cup says skyr or Greek yogurt. Comparing the nutrition panel per 100 g or per the same serving size prevents package size from creating a false winner.

Texture comes from concentration, but manufacturers can reach that texture in different ways. Traditional methods remove whey after fermentation, which raises the proportion of milk solids in the final spoonful. Some modern products may also adjust milk solids or use processing choices that produce a thick texture with less draining. That is why two tubs with the same style name can differ in protein, carbohydrate, calcium, and thickness. The ingredient list helps explain what the front label cannot.

Lactose is another area where simple rules fail. Straining removes some lactose with whey, and bacterial fermentation uses part of the milk sugar, so either skyr or Greek yogurt may contain less lactose than ordinary milk. But neither name automatically means lactose-free. People with lactose intolerance vary greatly in what they tolerate, and a flavored cup can contain extra carbohydrate from added sugars even when its natural lactose is modest. A lactose-free claim or a product-specific label is more useful than assuming one cultured dairy style is always easier to digest.

For everyday meals, choose around the role the food needs to play. A high-protein plain cup can work as breakfast with fruit and oats, as a snack, or as a base for sauces and dips. A fuller-fat Greek yogurt may bring a richer texture and more energy, while a very lean skyr can offer a large amount of protein for relatively few calories. Neither is automatically more nutritious in every diet; the best choice depends on protein needs, energy needs, taste, price, and whether added sugar is important to you.

Cultured dairy can also differ in acidity and mouthfeel. Skyr is often quite tangy and dense, while Greek yogurt can range from sharp and lean to rich and creamy depending on fat level. Those sensory differences change what toppings people add. A very tart low-fat cup may end up with more honey or granola than a richer unsweetened yogurt that is satisfying on its own, so the final bowl can reverse the calorie difference seen on the plain labels.

If sustainability or waste matters to you, packaging size and how reliably you finish the product may be worth considering alongside nutrition. A large tub can reduce packaging per serving but is not an advantage if half spoils. Buy the format that matches how often you actually use it.

What should decide the choice?

Check protein per serving, fat level and added sugar. If both are plain, either can be an efficient protein food. Texture and flavor may be the deciding factors.

faq.question: Which has more protein, skyr or Greek yogurt?
faq.answer: In these current plain products they are very close per 100 g: about 11.3 g for skyr and 10.6 g for FAGE Total 0%.

faq.question: Which has fewer calories?
faq.answer: The nonfat Greek yogurt example: about 53 versus 80 calories/100 g, largely because it has 0 g fat.

faq.question: Is all Greek yogurt nonfat?
faq.answer: No. FAGE currently offers 0%, 2% and 5% plain versions.

faq.question: Is skyr always higher in protein?
faq.answer: No. Both categories contain high-protein products, and labels should be compared directly.
